label: Linear Inequalities
overview: Linear inequalities are like equations but with <, >, ≤, or ≥ instead of =. The solution is a range of values, shown on a number line or coordinate plane. SAT questions ask you to solve one-variable inequalities, graph two-variable inequalities, identify solution regions, and work with compound inequalities (and / or).

keyFormulas.name: Compound AND
keyFormulas.latex: a < x < b \implies x \text{ is between } a \text{ and } b

keyFormulas.name: Compound OR
keyFormulas.latex: x < a \text{ or } x > b \implies \text{two separate rays}

steps.title: Divide by −2 and flip the inequality
steps.content: Dividing by a negative number reverses the direction.

steps.title: Interpret the solution
steps.content: All values of x less than or equal to −3 satisfy the inequality. On a number line, use a closed circle at −3 and shade left.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative
commonMistakes.fix: Any time you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality direction must reverse.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a closed circle (≤) when the inequality is strict (<)
commonMistakes.fix: Open circle means the endpoint is NOT included (<, >). Closed circle means it IS included (≤, ≥).

quickTip: Treat an inequality exactly like an equation until you need to multiply or divide by a negative — that's the only step that's different. Check your answer by plugging in a test value from your solution set.
